Make your hips push your feet into the floor, that's it. That single focus is usually enough to take the low back completely out of the equation when you sit or stand.

Here's why it works: your low back muscles don't push your foot. Everybody knows that. So the moment you shift your attention to foot pressure, the body stops recruiting the spine to do the job and starts letting the glutes, hamstrings, and quads take over, the muscles that were supposed to be doing this all along.

If you have a disc herniation, this is where our team starts. Try it on your next sit-to-stand.

More in the full article. Link in bio 👆

samples.transcript:
Clinician: # An Hour Can Change Your Life

Most people managing chronic pain or a 'next-step surgery' have never been given a real hour of focused assessment. Here's what changes when they are.

That’s not a tagline. It’s just what I’ve watched happen, over and over, for years.

Someone comes in. They’ve been told their knee is bone-on-bone. They’ve been told surgery is the next step. They’ve been managing — or not managing — pain for so long it’s become the background noise of their life. They’ve stopped hiking, or skiing, or playing with their grandkids, because that’s just what happens when you get older, right?

Then we spend an hour together.

Not on a waiting list. Not getting another scan. An actual hour of assessment, movement, and conversation about what their body is doing and why. And most of the time — not always, but most of the time — we find something. A pattern we can change. A load we can redistribute. A movement the nervous system has been avoiding that, once we address it, changes the whole picture.

No surgery. No medication. No giving up on the sports and activities that make life feel like life.

I know that sounds too simple. But simple isn’t the same as easy to find.

The medical system, for all it does well, isn’t built for this. It’s built for acute problems, pathology, high-stakes decisions. It’s not designed to sit with someone and ask: what do you actually want to be able to do? And then figure out how to get you there.

That’s what we built Move Better for.

What I hear constantly from patients is that nobody in the healthcare system has ever worked with them the way we do. Not the time we take. Not the way we look at the problem. And most of them come in skeptical — because they’ve been through the system, they’ve been told what’s wrong, and they’ve been told the goal is to make it manageable.

We think the bar should be higher than manageable.

Fall risk is a big one. The literature on falls — the injuries, the loss of independence, the downstream consequences — it’s brutal. And falls are, in most cases, preventable. Not with caution and handrails and giving up on stairs. With training. With understanding what the body is actually doing and addressing it directly.

Same with surgeries people are told are inevitable. I’m not saying surgery is never the right answer. But I’ve watched too many people get to a point where someone finally looked at the whole picture, worked on the actual problem, and avoided a procedure they’d already scheduled. That doesn’t make headlines. It just happens quietly, in a gym or a treatment room, without any announcement.

Here’s what I know from doing this work: we can reduce people’s suffering if we can just get an hour with them. It’s easy, and repeatable, and reliable — when you actually understand what you’re working with.

The hard part isn’t the hour. The hard part is getting people to believe it’s worth trying.

If you’ve been managing pain, managing a limitation, managing the gap between what you want to do and what you’ve been told you’re allowed to do — come in. One hour to find out whether what you’re dealing with is actually as permanent as someone told you it was.

Most of the time, it isn’t.

The vast majority of patients that come into our clinic with an MRI confirmed disc herniation will make a full recovery with more conservative interventions like movement-based treatment.

What that actually means in practice: focusing less on fixing the structure of the disc herniation, and more so figuring out the behavioral and stabilization and movement patterns that led to the stress that caused the herniation in the first place.

The scan shows the disc. It doesn't show the pattern that loaded it.

Bernard: Hey Dr. Sophie, Bernard here — thanks for making the time. Let's dig into this.

First question, and it's a big one to start with: when someone comes in with bicep tendinopathy, what's the underlying principle that guides how you approach it? Not the specific tools you use, but the *why* behind them — what are you actually trying to solve?
Clinician: when someone comes in with biceps tendinopathy  we're trying to solve why did it happen so why did the bicep why is the bicep being overloaded or why is the tendon being compressed what's the root cause of the irritation in the tendon  while the times we're going to start looking at okay well how does the scapula move across the body when it's going into retraction so  that's going to be looking at the thoracic spine Mobility sometimes it is not necessarily like week rotator cuff musculature but maybe the coordination of the strength of the rotator cuff  sometimes it happens in the like setup or the the actual activity that they're doing and how they're doing the activity the mechanics of the movement so the patient comes in with a pain in the front of the shoulder or  and let's say that they're having it with like bench pressing is pretty common then I would have them set up the bench press and I'm just going to look at the mechanics of their press and what kind of kinetic chain things can I see sometimes I have to look at it like the mobility of the wrist or the elbow and how all that stuff kind of plays into what's being expressed at the shoulder so
Bernard: Makes sense — you're essentially reverse-engineering the pain to find where the system broke down upstream. 

When you're watching someone set up a bench press or do whatever movement is provoking it, what's the most common thing you actually *see* that's driving the overload? Like if you had to name the culprit that shows up most often, what is it?
Clinician: most often  the ability to create or have extension in the thoracic spine  the thoracic spine already doesn't have that much extension  so when you're setting up your bench press if you don't have that extension makes it really hard for the shoulder blades to to like retract and then that retraction can create some like anterior tilting of the shoulder blade and then that creates compression over the front of the joint and sometimes it's a like  mobility issue of the shoulders whether that's like an internal rotation or an external rotation a lot of times I find that people have the passive ability to get into those ranges but they don't have like active strength to get into those ranges  so if you're doing something like bench pressing which  requires both then and more specifically what I see is people don't have the active like external rotation strength to be able to maintain the bench press position  so that's what kind of creates the  reduced ability to like retract the shoulders so that's probably the most common thing it's just the mobility of the shoulder blades and the thoracic spine and then how they interact with each other
Bernard: Got it. So it's less about the bicep itself and more about what's happening two or three joints up the chain — the thoracic spine and scapula just aren't doing their job, and the bicep tendon ends up paying the price.

Clinician: yeah a lot of patients try to when they come in they're like yeah I've been stretching my shoulder a lot this pain doesn't go away or they'll say yeah I took a couple days of rest the pain went away and then I just went back to bench pressing again so the biggest misconception is that it's actually just a capacity problem of the shoulder blade as well sorry if the biceps tendon  so the bicep tendon is actually a big stabilizer of the shoulder so  we need strength in the biceps tendon like it needs to be strong to stabilize the shoulder itself  and so I think people are sometimes surprised that it's like no we're actually going to strengthen the biceps tendon we just need to give it the appropriate load and build its strength up with Progressive overload versus just resting or stretching it which does nothing to increase the actual capacity of the tendon  so that's probably the biggest thing that people have a misconception about
Bernard: [AGREEMENT]

That lines up with something several of your colleagues here have mentioned — that the instinct to rest and stretch is actually working against recovery, and that building strength through progressive load is the real mechanism. Does that match your experience, or do you find there are cases where even that framing needs a caveat?
Clinician: that's a good question  sometimes  to that could be  maybe we use like stretching in a more active sense to open up the the chest or the packs or create that extension in the thoracic spine  and then  and then that's going to allow us to have kind of like a pain-free window where we can actually build strength so they probably isn't really like a caveat to you just need to stretch the tendon it's going to feel better but maybe stretch the areas like around that area  yeah but yeah usually it's just we need to build strength in the tissue and kind of clean up the range of motion some of the other areas
Bernard: [AGREEMENT]

Right, so the stretching isn't useless — it's just aimed at the *wrong place* when people are doing it to the tendon itself. Opening up the thoracic spine and pecs to create the conditions where you can actually load well. That's a meaningful distinction.

So when a patient hears "we're going to strengthen your bicep tendon" — what's the look on their face usually? Because I'm guessing that feels pretty counterintuitive when the thing hurts.
Clinician: yeah I think it's pretty counterintuitive to strengthen  or like use the thing that hurts but  usually when you just kind of  talk to them and describe it as being a capacity issue  then and you can kind of like verbalize that to them I think it helps a lot but yeah I think and something is painful loading it with weight usually isn't the first thing that people think about  but I also like to find ways to load like the the actual like long head of the tendon in the more like proximal setting and sometimes doing that and then also showing people how to create proper  like proper scapular retraction in those moments can be really useful as well  but yeah it's usually pretty counterintuitive to think that we need to strengthen the thing that hurts sometimes too if you can  like do a movement that's going to strengthen it or provide load to the tendon  it's like at an appropriate level and you can show people like hey like like you're doing this thing and then it starts to feel better sometimes that helps too  yeah that's kind of a situation where maybe actions speak a little louder than words
